newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem, Serb refugees vote in strategic town.
newsitem.headline: Moslem, Serb refugees vote in strategic town.

text.p: Bosnian Serb refugees and Moslems expelled from the Serb-controlled town of Doboj in 1992 came together to vote on Saturday, highlighting the complexities of Bosnia's election.

Serbs who had no interest in the town but who said they had been directed to vote there by Serb authorities reacted in sharp contrast to Moslem refugees who strained to catch a glimpse of the homes they once occupied.
Dusan, 70, and Ljubisa, 65, came to Doboj to vote from northern Serbia where they settled after their home towns in western Bosnia were captured by Croat troops in an offensive last year.
They were among an estimated 19,000 Serbs bussed into the town from across Bosnia and Serbia to vote.

Refugees and displaced people were allowed to vote in any Bosnian town where they intend to live at a later date, to give them the opportunity to influence the election outcome in their possible future home.
But Dusan said he would return to Serbia where his family lived. "I have no job, no means to live here, so I'll live with my daughters in Novi Sad."
Observers believe Bosnian Serb authorities manipulated displaced Serb voters by sending them to vote in strategic towns they wanted to keep under control.

Municipal elections in the Bosnian Serb Republic were cancelled because of irregularities in voter registration, but voters will still elect local representatives to a national parliamentary assembly.
The Doboj area had more than 40,000 Moslems and fewer than 30,000 Serbs before the war. Now only 1,000 Moslems remain in the town, with 70,000 Serbs.

While Dusan and Ljubisa quietly sipped their beer after casting their votes, busses brought several hundred Doboj Moslems back to town, for a brief, strictly-controlled visit, during which they were to vote.
Many looked wistfully around, watching for familiar signs in the town they fled in panic four years ago.
Most of them, now living in Croat-Moslem territory only a few kilometres from Doboj, are determined to return to the town to live, even if that means living alongside the Serbs.

"We can live with the Serbs. We don't mind them and we never hated them. Now, what they think of us I can't say," said Bahrudin Didic, 45. "We hope the elections will be fair and we shall soon return."
His wife, Fikreta, 42, managed to slip away from numerous Serb guards, who politely but firmly rejected refugees' pleas to "just set an eye on their old homes".
She hurried to her abandoned house on a hill above the town and burst into tears on the threshold, burying her head in her hands.

"My god, will I ever return here? This is my life's work and now it's gone...Let all the Serbs stay here, if they want to. But then their authorities should build new houses for them, so I can return to mine," she said, sobbing.
